newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China '97 soybean imports to drop -- oilseeds study.
newsitem.headline: China '97 soybean imports to drop -- oilseeds study.

text.p: China will import 800,000 tonnes of soybeans in 1997, down from one million tonnes in 1996, according to a study on China's oilseeds industry sponsored by the American Soybean Association (ASA).

The study said higher production in 1997 would constrain imports. China's 1997 soybean production was expected to jump to 13.93 million tonnes from 12.17 million tonnes in 1996 and 13.5 million tonnes in 1995, it said.
But the scope of increase was limited, pointing to a long-term trend toward shortage, the ASA-sponsored study said.
"The largest constraint on soybean production is the constant competition for land with grain crops," said the study seen in Hong Kong on Tuesday.
Large-scale soybean acreage expansion was impossible and any production increase would come from yield improvement, it said.

But some Hong Kong-based traders said the real constraint on China's soybean production was a provincial government policy banning export of soybeans outside the northeastern province of Heilongjiang, China's largest soybean production area.
"It keeps soybean prices artifically low, making it cheaper for the government to buy its own quota, but reduces farmers' incentives to plant soybeans," one senior grains trader said.

The ASA-sponsored study said China's low soybean production meant the supply shortage would continue over the next few years. "Some crushers find it difficult to get quality beans domestically, thus are eager to import," it said.

China's total soybean supply in this year totalled 24.09 million tonnes, with 10.91 million tonnes of carryin from the previous year and 12.17 million tonnes in production complemented by one million tonnes in imports, the study said.

In the study, total soybean consumption in 1996 was pegged at 14.11 million tonnes, including 8.10 million tonnes destined for the crushing industry, 4.89 million tonnes for food and industrial use and 300,000 tonnes in exports, with 9.97 million tonnes as carryout.

"In the long run, China's oilseed production will continue to increase," the study said, noting at in 1995 oilseed production was at 42.88 million tonnes and would jump to 50 million tonnes by the year 2000.
"Because of the impact of oil imports, production may wander or drop from the 1995-level in the next few years," it said.
China imported a total of 3.58 million tonnes of vegetable oils in 1995, with 1.48 million tonnes of soyoil, 630,000 tonnes of rapeseed oil and 1.39 million tonnes of palm oil, it said.
China's rapeseed production in 1996 was estimated at 8.82 million tonnes and was projected to drop to 7.96 million tonnes in 1997 before recovering to 9.61 million tonnes in 1998.

"Due to the large quantity of oil imports, (rapeseed) acreage will continue to decline in 1997, and may start to recover in 1998," the study said, adding that land idle in winter in the south could possibly be planted with rapeseed to increase production.
Peanut production is also expected to drop, from 9.72 million tonnes in 1996 to 8.78 million tonnes in 1997, suffering in the competition against grain.
China's crushing capacity had grown from 35 million tonnes in 1990 to 60 million tonnes in 1995, about 1.5 times the total domestic oilseed supply, the report said.
"Because of the overcapacity in the crushing industry, plants were forced to crush other oilseeds to increase facility utilization," the report said.
